summary: Lists a selection of characters, with mnemonics, and their presence in several coded character sets. It is informational and helps people compare character sets.

eli5.summary: A chart of letters and symbols, with short nicknames, that shows which of the different computer alphabets contain each one.

questions: how many character sets does rfc 1345 cover
subtitle: A standardized system for referring to characters across all human writing systems

tldr.problem: The Internet was originally built for English text, but has expanded globally. Without a standard way to refer to characters and identify which writing systems contain them, international mail and protocols cannot reliably represent text beyond ASCII.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1345 defines two-character mnemonics for characters in Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic, Hebrew, and Asian scripts, and variable-length codes for ideographic characters. It then maps these mnemonics to character values across all major character sets—ISO 8859 variants, EBCDIC, vendor character sets, and East Asian encodings.
tldr.outcome: Internet standards now have an unambiguous way to refer to specific characters, and developers can compare how different character sets represent the same symbols. This foundation enabled later standards for international email and web content.

facts.label: Two-character mnemonics
facts.value: One for each accented Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic, Hebrew character

today: RFC 1345 is Informational and predates modern Unicode/UTF-8, which eventually solved the character set problem more comprehensively. However, the mnemonic system and character mapping remain a useful reference for understanding legacy systems and for protocols that still need to refer to characters by name rather than code point.

sections.title: The Internationalization Challenge
sections.content:
The Internet's core protocols were designed around ASCII, a 7-bit character set sufficient for English text. As the Internet expanded globally, the Internet community needed a way to represent the writing systems of other countries: accented Latin letters for European languages, Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic, Hebrew, and the ideographic characters of Chinese, Japanese, and Korean.

The problem was two-fold: first, no standard way existed to unambiguously refer to a specific character in an Internet standard; second, there was no reliable mapping showing which characters appear in which character sets. RFC 1345 solves both problems by defining a universal mnemonic system for characters and documenting how these characters are encoded in over 100 different character sets.
sections.eli5: Computers in France, Japan, and Greece all use different letter sets. Without a shared way to name a letter, it's hard for them to talk about what character they mean.

sections.title: The Mnemonic System
sections.content:
The RFC defines two categories of mnemonics. Two-character mnemonics are used for characters in most writing systems: Latin (including accented letters), Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic, and Hebrew. These mnemonics are designed to visually resemble the character they represent, within the constraints of the ASCII base set. For example, A' is Latin capital A with acute accent, and A! is A with grave accent. After a base letter, the second character indicates the diacritical mark: ' means acute, > means circumflex, ? means tilde, and so on.

Variable-length mnemonics are used for characters where visual similarity is not practical—primarily the tens of thousands of ideographic characters in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. These use a character set identifier (like j for JIS X0208) followed by row and column numbers. All mnemonics are built from the invariant subset of ISO 646—a set of 83 characters guaranteed to exist in the same form across all ASCII variants and EBCDIC implementations.
sections.eli5: A mnemonic is like a nickname. 'A-acute' becomes 'A'' (using ASCII only). For Chinese characters, we use numbers from the official character standard table.

sections.title: Character Set Coverage
sections.content:
RFC 1345 documents approximately 100 character sets, organized into families. The ISO 8859 family provides eight different 8-bit character sets: ISO 8859-1 (Latin-1, Western European), ISO 8859-5 (Cyrillic), ISO 8859-6 (Arabic), ISO 8859-8 (Hebrew), and variants for Greek, Baltic, and other regions. Each adds 128 characters to the base 128-character ASCII set to support a different language or region.

Beyond ISO standards, the RFC covers many vendor-specific character sets: IBM PC codepages, various EBCDIC variants used in mainframes, and character sets from computer manufacturers like DEC, HP, and Apple. It also includes the East Asian 16-bit character sets: GB 2312-1980 (Chinese), JIS X0208 and JIS X0212 (Japanese), and KS C 5601 (Korean). For each character, the RFC provides its code value in the character set, its mnemonic, its long descriptive name from ISO standards, and its position in ISO 10646 (the emerging Unicode standard).
sections.eli5: The memo is like a Rosetta Stone for computers: it shows the same letter in 100 different alphabets and languages.

sections.title: Mnemonic Character Sets and Registration
sections.content:
The RFC defines the concept of a mnemonic character set—an extension of any given character set to include all characters defined in RFC 1345. This allows a system using, say, ISO 8859-1 to encode any character from any other set by using the mnemonic escape convention. If a character is not in the native character set, the ampersand character (&) serves as an intro, followed by the mnemonic, followed by a semicolon. This allows messages to include characters that are not natively supported while remaining unambiguous.

All character set names defined in RFC 1345 are registered with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), so they can be referenced unambiguously in Internet standards and protocols. The RFC also specifies the conditions for registering new character sets with IANA as new writing systems or vendor encodings are discovered or created.
sections.eli5: Once a character has a nickname, any computer program can ask for it by name, even if that character isn't built into its native alphabet.

sections.title: Practical Application and Impact
sections.content:
RFC 1345 serves as both a reference for Internet standards and a practical tool for developers. Standards can refer to characters by mnemonic (e.g., 'the A' character') instead of listing numeric codes, which makes the standard readable to humans and unambiguous to machines. This was especially important for protocols like MIME, which needed to specify character sets and encoding, and for internationalized email standards that came later.

The mnemonics are also used as a fallback representation in systems where the native character set does not support all characters needed. A user agent could display '&=e'' if the user's font does not include the é character, or use mnemonics in system logs and debugging output to represent international text in a form that all systems can display. This principle influenced later standards for internationalized domain names, email, and web protocols.
sections.eli5: When an old computer that only knows English encounters a fancy French letter, it can show the pattern '&e'' instead, and anyone who knows the rules can understand what it means.
